blocks.heading: Linking the accounting concepts
blocks.text: Income and expenses describe financial performance over a period, while assets, liabilities and owner’s equity describe financial position at a date. Gross profit is sales revenue less cost of sales; net profit is gross profit plus other income less other expenses in a simple trading statement. Owner’s equity is the residual interest after liabilities are deducted from assets. Drawings withdraw value for a sole owner’s personal use and reduce equity; they are not an operating expense. Capital employed is the long-term finance in use, measured here as owner’s capital plus non-current liabilities. Employment of capital concerns where finance is invested in assets, rather than the number of employees. Working capital is current assets less current liabilities. A loan creates cash and a liability, not trading income. A machine purchase exchanges one asset for another rather than making its full price an immediate ordinary expense in this simple distinction. Keep the type of transaction clear before deciding where it belongs.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri Traders: annual turnover N$240,000, cost of sales N$144,000, other expenses N$72,000, credit sales N$219,000 and credit purchases N$146,000. At year end: non-current assets N$90,000; inventory N$30,000; debtors N$18,000; cash N$12,000; current liabilities N$30,000 (including creditors N$20,000); non-current liabilities N$40,000; owner’s equity N$80,000. Opening inventory was N$18,000. Use the opening and closing inventory average for inventory turnover. No other income or expense is assumed in this simple example. Neri has gross profit N$96,000 and net profit N$24,000. Its total assets are N$150,000 and total liabilities N$70,000, leaving equity N$80,000. Capital employed is N$120,000 and working capital N$30,000. The same business therefore has several different financial measures, each answering a different question.

blocks.heading: Income
blocks.text: Income is value earned by the business during a period, including sales revenue and any other specified income. In a trading example turnover is sales revenue. Income need not be received immediately in cash: a credit sale can create a debtor. A new owner contribution or loan receipt supplies finance but is not income earned from selling goods or services.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Eta Goods makes N$8,000 credit sales and borrows N$5,000. The sales are trading income; the loan is finance creating a liability. Treating both as sales would overstate performance.

blocks.heading: Expenses
blocks.text: Expenses are costs charged against income for a period when measuring profit. Examples include rent, wages and interest for that period. Paying cash is not enough to classify a transaction as an expense: buying a machine creates an asset and repaying loan principal reduces a liability. A cost can be charged as an expense before or after the related cash payment.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Lara Prints pays monthly rent N$2,000 and buys equipment costing N$10,000. Rent is an expense for the month. The equipment purchase is an asset acquisition; it is not automatically a N$10,000 ordinary monthly expense.

blocks.heading: Gross profit
blocks.text: Gross profit is sales revenue less cost of sales for the period. Cost of sales concerns the goods sold, not all operating expenses. In a simple trader it is opening inventory plus purchases less closing inventory, using the figures specified. Gross profit is a money amount; gross profit margin expresses it relative to sales as a percentage.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has annual turnover N$240,000 and cost of sales N$144,000. Gross profit is N$96,000. Rent and other expenses still need to be considered before finding net profit.

blocks.heading: Net profit
blocks.text: Net profit is the surplus after the relevant expenses have been deducted from income. In the simple trading model, start with gross profit, add other income if any and deduct other expenses. A loss occurs when relevant expenses exceed income. Net profit is not the business’s cash balance and is distinct from net profit margin, which relates it to turnover.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has gross profit N$96,000 and other expenses N$72,000, with no other income. Net profit is N$24,000. This does not prove that N$24,000 is immediately available to spend because income and payments can have different timing.

blocks.heading: Capital employed
blocks.text: Capital employed is the long-term finance in use in the business. In Annexe A it is owner’s capital plus long-term liabilities; with a consistent Statement of Financial Position it also equals total assets less current liabilities. It is the denominator for ROCE in this syllabus. Use year-end figures unless instructed otherwise, rather than silently substituting a different average.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has owner’s equity N$80,000 and non-current liabilities N$40,000. Capital employed is N$120,000. Its N$30,000 current liabilities are not added to this long-term-finance definition.

blocks.heading: Employment of capital
blocks.text: Employment of capital concerns how the business uses finance in assets and operations. Sources explain where finance comes from; employment explains where it is invested, for example machinery, inventory and receivables. It does not mean the number of jobs created. A productive asset base can still leave insufficient immediately available cash if funds are tied up in slow-moving stock.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri holds non-current assets N$90,000 and current assets N$60,000. These identify uses of resources, while owner’s equity and liabilities explain financing claims. A machine is employment of finance, not a new provider of finance.

blocks.heading: Owner’s equity
blocks.text: Owner’s equity is the owner’s residual interest in the business’s assets after deducting liabilities. The accounting relationship is assets less liabilities equals equity. Contributions and retained profit can increase it, while drawings reduce it in a sole-owner example. Equity is not necessarily cash: the corresponding assets may include equipment and amounts customers owe.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has total assets N$150,000 and total liabilities N$70,000. Equity is N$80,000. The owner cannot infer that the business has N$80,000 cash from this residual figure.

blocks.heading: Drawings
blocks.text: Drawings are money or other value taken from the business by its sole owner for personal use. They reduce owner’s equity and, for cash drawings, reduce business cash. They are not an ordinary business expense incurred to earn sales, so they do not reduce trading profit in the same way as rent or wages. Distinguish owner withdrawals from a payment to an employee for work.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional sole trader takes N$2,000 from business cash to buy personal groceries. Record drawings and reduced cash, not wages or cost of sales. Calling it an expense would misstate the business’s operating performance.

blocks.heading: Non-current assets
blocks.text: Non-current assets are resources held for continuing use in business operations rather than expected short-term conversion in ordinary trading. Examples include premises, machinery and delivery equipment. Their accounting value is not necessarily what a buyer would pay immediately. An asset’s purpose matters: a vehicle held for repeated deliveries differs from a vehicle held as stock by a dealer.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Oka Supply uses a van repeatedly for deliveries and holds packaged goods for sale. The van is a non-current asset; goods for sale are inventory within current assets. A high van value does not make it immediately spendable money.

blocks.heading: Current assets
blocks.text: Current assets are resources expected to be realised, sold or used within the normal operating cycle or short term, such as inventory, debtors and cash. They differ in liquidity: cash is immediately available, debtors must pay and inventory must be sold. The total is therefore not an immediately available bank balance.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has inventory N$30,000, debtors N$18,000 and cash N$12,000. Current assets total N$60,000. Only the stated N$12,000 is already cash; the rest depends on conversion and collection.

blocks.heading: Liabilities
blocks.text: Liabilities are obligations the business owes to others. Current liabilities fall due in the short term, while non-current liabilities are longer-term obligations. Supplier creditors and an agreed short-term overdraft are common current examples; a long-term loan can be non-current. Classify any portion falling due soon appropriately when the question supplies it. A liability is not an asset simply because borrowing brought cash into the business.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has current liabilities N$30,000 and non-current liabilities N$40,000. Total liabilities are N$70,000. The N$30,000 is relevant to current and quick ratios, whereas solvency compares assets with the full N$70,000.

blocks.heading: Working capital
blocks.text: Working capital is current assets less current liabilities. It indicates net short-term resources supporting day-to-day operations. Positive working capital is not proof of available cash because inventory or debtors may be slow to turn into money. Insufficient working capital can make paying near-term commitments difficult even if long-term assets are valuable. Working capital is a money amount, distinct from the current ratio.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has current assets N$60,000 and current liabilities N$30,000. Working capital is N$30,000. The current ratio is 2.00:1, a different format relating the same two totals; neither makes all current assets cash.
